title: Retry topologies
summary: Delayed retries with TTL and dead-letter exchanges in RabbitMQ, retry topics and a DLT in Kafka and what they do to ordering, delivery limits across brokers and the parking lot.

steps.title: Delayed retry in RabbitMQ: TTL + DLX
body: RabbitMQ has no "deliver this in 10 seconds". You build it from two features: a **wait queue** with a message
TTL and no consumers, whose dead-letter target is the work queue.
```text
nack(requeue: false)                       TTL 10 s expires
│      (DLX "" → routing key         no consumers            (DLX "" → routing key "orders")
│       "orders.retry.10s")
└─ after 3 attempts the consumer publishes to orders.parking-lot and acks instead
```csharp fragment
await channel.QueueDeclareAsync("orders", durable: true, exclusive: false, autoDelete: false,
arguments: new Dictionary<string, object?>
["x-queue-type"] = "quorum",
["x-dead-letter-exchange"] = "",
["x-dead-letter-routing-key"] = "orders.retry.10s",
await channel.QueueDeclareAsync("orders.retry.10s", durable: true, exclusive: false, autoDelete: false,
arguments: new Dictionary<string, object?>
["x-queue-type"] = "quorum",
["x-message-ttl"] = 10_000,
["x-dead-letter-exchange"] = "",
["x-dead-letter-routing-key"] = "orders",
Each trip adds to the message's `x-death` header; the entry for `orders.retry.10s` with reason `expired`
counts the retries so far. For backoff, use one wait queue **per delay tier** (10 s, 1 min, 10 min).
Quorum queues dead-letter *at most once* by default; set `dead-letter-strategy: at-least-once` (with
`overflow: reject-publish`) when a retry must not vanish during a failover.
> **See it:** **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ**, challenge *Retry later, not now*.

steps.prompt: Put the life of a message that fails three times in order (3 attempts allowed).
lines: Attempt 1 fails; the consumer nacks with `requeue: false`
It waits there, unconsumed, until its 10 s TTL expires
`orders.retry.10s` dead-letters it back to `orders`; its `x-death` count for that queue is now 1
Attempt 2 fails and the same cycle runs again
Attempt 3 fails; the consumer publishes it to `orders.parking-lot` and acks the original
steps.explain: The wait happens inside the broker, so the consumer never sleeps and the rest of the queue keeps flowing. The consumer reads the attempt number from `x-death` to know when to stop.

steps.prompt: A team uses **one** retry queue and sets the delay per message with `Expiration` (`"300000"` for some messages, `"5000"` for others). The 5-second retries take up to 5 minutes. Why?
options: Messages only expire when they reach the head of the queue, so a 5 s message waits behind a 5 min one
Per-message TTL is rounded up to the largest TTL in the queue
The retry queue has no consumer, so expiry is paused
steps.explain: RabbitMQ expires messages from the head. Mixed per-message TTLs in one queue block each other: use one queue per delay tier with a queue-level `x-message-ttl`. (A delayed-message exchange plugin exists, with its own limits; the tiered queues are the portable answer.)

steps.title: Retries in Kafka: retry topics and a DLT
body: Kafka has no per-message ack or requeue: committing offset 42 means "everything before 42 is done". A failing
record leaves two choices:
```text
orders            P0 | 40 | 41 | 42 | 43 |       the consumer fails on 41
└─> orders.retry-1   consumer waits until record time + 10 s
└─> orders.retry-2   + 1 min
└─> orders.dlt   people look, replay later
- **Blocking retry**: retry 41 in place (`consumer.Seek` back to it, `consumer.Pause` the partition while you
wait). Order is kept, but the whole partition stalls behind one record.
- **Non-blocking retry**: produce 41 to `orders.retry-1`, commit, carry on with 42. The partition keeps
flowing, but **order for that key is broken**: a later update for the same order may be applied first.
A retry-topic consumer must not sleep in its poll loop longer than `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes by
default) or the group evicts it; it pauses the partition and resumes when the record is due. Spring's
`@RetryableTopic` implements this pattern; in .NET you write it (or use a messaging framework). When order
matters, route **later records for a key already in retry** to the retry topic too.
> **See it:** **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, challenge *Committed, then crashed*: it shows why the offset may only be committed after a record is processed (or safely handed to a retry topic).

items: Order status changes applied with no version check
Search index updates that carry a version and skip older ones
Seat reservations where the first request wins
steps.explain: If applying two records for the same key in the wrong order gives a wrong result, keep order. If the handler is order-independent (or a version check makes it so), keep the partition flowing.

steps.prompt: The first attempt at `o17:v1` fails and it goes to a retry topic, which succeeds later. What is applied, in order?
steps.explain: Order 17 ends at version 1: the stale update arrived last and overwrote the newer one. That is the price of non-blocking retries without a version check.

steps.title: Delivery limits and parking lots, broker by broker
body: Every platform has a knob that says "stop trying":
| Platform | Knob | Where the message goes |
| RabbitMQ quorum queue | `delivery-limit` policy (default 20 since 4.0) | its DLX, or dropped without one |
| Azure Service Bus | `MaxDeliveryCount` (default 10) | the entity's `$DeadLetterQueue` sub-queue, with `DeadLetterReason` |
| AWS SQS | redrive policy `maxReceiveCount` | the DLQ in `deadLetterTargetArn`; the visibility timeout decides when a receive counts again |
| Google Cloud Pub/Sub | dead-letter policy `maxDeliveryAttempts` (5 to 100) | the dead-letter topic |
| Kafka | nothing built in | your own retry topics and DLT; count attempts in a header |
A **DLQ** catches what the broker gave up on. A **parking lot** is where *your* code puts a message after its
retries are used up or the error is permanent. Neither has an automatic consumer: people triage them, fix the
cause, and redrive (next lesson). Keep the original body plus headers that explain it: the error, the
exception type, the attempt count and the original queue or topic.

steps.prompt: Match each platform to its "stop retrying" knob.
pairs: None: count in a header and produce to a DLT yourself
steps.explain: The names differ, the idea does not: a bounded number of attempts, then a place where a person will look.

steps.title: Read the retry count from x-death
prompt: **Symptom first.** After a client upgrade the order consumer crashes on every retried message:
```text
System.InvalidCastException: Unable to cast object of type 'System.Byte[]' to type 'System.String'.
at Orders.Retry.RetryCount(IDictionary`2 headers, String retryQueue)
AMQP sends header strings as bytes, and RabbitMQ.Client hands them to you as `byte[]` (UTF-8), not `string`.
Arrays arrive as lists, tables as dictionaries, numbers such as `count` as `long`.
Fix `long RetryCount(IDictionary<string, object?>? headers, string retryQueue)`: return the `count` of the
`x-death` entry whose `queue` is `retryQueue` and whose `reason` is `"expired"`; `0` if there are no headers,
no `x-death`, or no such entry. Accept `queue` and `reason` as either `byte[]` or `string`.
starter: long RetryCount(IDictionary<string, object?>? headers, string retryQueue)
if (headers is null || !headers.TryGetValue("x-death", out var raw)) return 0;
solution: long RetryCount(IDictionary<string, object?>? headers, string retryQueue)
if (headers is null || !headers.TryGetValue("x-death", out var raw) || raw is not IEnumerable<object> deaths) return 0;
if (item is not IDictionary<string, object?> death) continue;
return death.TryGetValue("count", out var c) && c is long n ? n : 0;
static string? Text(IDictionary<string, object?> d, string key) =>
d.TryGetValue(key, out var v) ? v switch { byte[] b => Encoding.UTF8.GetString(b), string s => s, _ => null } : null;
hints: Do not cast; test the type: `v switch { byte[] b => Encoding.UTF8.GetString(b), string s => s, _ => null }`.
Use `raw is not IEnumerable<object> deaths` and `item is not IDictionary<string, object?> death` to skip anything unexpected.
template: new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["queue"] = DojoBytes("orders.retry.10s"), ["reason"] = DojoBytes("expired"), ["count"] = 3L, ["exchange"] = DojoBytes("") },
new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["queue"] = DojoBytes("orders"), ["reason"] = DojoBytes("rejected"), ["count"] = 3L, ["exchange"] = DojoBytes("") },
Dojo.Eq("reads the count from byte[] values", 3L, RetryCount(dojoHeaders, "orders.retry.10s"));
Dojo.Eq("no entry for another wait queue", 0L, RetryCount(dojoHeaders, "orders.retry.1m"));
Dojo.Eq("a rejected entry is not a retry", 0L, RetryCount(dojoHeaders, "orders"));
Dojo.Eq("first delivery: no x-death yet", 0L, RetryCount(new Dictionary<string, object?>(), "orders.retry.10s"));

steps.title: A tiered retry consumer on a fake clock
prompt: Simulate TTL retry tiers and a parking lot, deterministically.
Write a class `RetryingConsumer`:
- `RetryingConsumer(Func<string, int, string> handler, long[] tierDelaysMs)`: `handler(id, attempt)` returns
`"ok"`, `"transient"` or `"permanent"`. Tier `i` is the wait before attempt `i + 2`.
- `void Publish(string id, long atMs)`: the message is due at `atMs`, as attempt 1.
- `List<string> RunUntil(long untilMs)`: repeatedly take the due message (due time `<= untilMs`) with the
**earliest due time**, ties in the order they were scheduled, and call the handler at its due time `t`:
- `"ok"` → log `"{t} {id} #{attempt} ok"`;
- `"transient"` with a tier left (`attempt <= tiers`) → schedule attempt + 1 at `t + delay` and log
`"{t} {id} #{attempt} transient -> retry in {delay} ms"`;
- `"transient"` with no tier left, or `"permanent"` → add the id to `ParkingLot` and log
`"{t} {id} #{attempt} {outcome} -> parking lot"`.
Return the log of this run. Messages due later stay scheduled for the next run.
- `List<string> ParkingLot` (get-only).
starter: public RetryingConsumer(Func<string, int, string> handler, long[] tierDelaysMs) { }
public void Publish(string id, long atMs) { }
solution: readonly List<(long At, long Seq, string Id, int Attempt)> scheduled = new();
public RetryingConsumer(Func<string, int, string> handler, long[] tierDelaysMs)
public void Publish(string id, long atMs) => scheduled.Add((atMs, seq++, id, 1));
var due = scheduled.Where(s => s.At <= untilMs).OrderBy(s => s.At).ThenBy(s => s.Seq).ToList();
hints: Keep a list of `(long At, long Seq, string Id, int Attempt)` and a running sequence number for ties.
Each loop: pick the earliest due entry with `OrderBy(At).ThenBy(Seq)`, remove it, handle it, maybe reschedule.
template: string DojoHandler(string id, int attempt) => id switch
var dojoC = new RetryingConsumer(DojoHandler, new long[] { 1000, 5000 });
Dojo.Eq("parked in the order they gave up", new List<string> { "d", "c" }, dojoC.ParkingLot);
var dojoP = new RetryingConsumer(DojoHandler, new long[] { 1000 });
Dojo.Eq("a run stops at its time limit", new List<string> { "0 b #1 transient -> retry in 1000 ms" }, dojoP.RunUntil(500));
Dojo.Eq("nothing due yet", new List<string>(), dojoP.RunUntil(999));
Dojo.Eq("the retry runs when it is due", new List<string> { "1000 b #2 ok" }, dojoP.RunUntil(2000));
var dojoN = new RetryingConsumer(DojoHandler, new long[0]);
Dojo.Eq("no tiers: a transient failure is parked at once", new List<string> { "5 c #1 transient -> parking lot" }, dojoN.RunUntil(5));
